title: Celestial Writing (Scriptura coelestis)
otherNames: Angelic script / Angelic alphabet (modern websites, e.g. Omniglot; not Agrippa's name for it)
family: Hebrew-based ring-letter (charaktêres / 'Brillenbuchstaben') alphabets: sister of Malachim and Transitus fluvii (Passing the River)
summary: The Celestial Writing is a 22-letter alphabet, one letter for each Hebrew letter, made of thin strokes that end in small rings. Agrippa printed it in De occulta philosophia, Book III, chapter 30 (first complete edition, [Cologne], July 1533), alongside Malachim and Passing the River. Agrippa does not claim it as his own: he reports that the Hebrews call it 'celestial' because they show it placed and figured among the stars, as astrologers draw the images of the signs from the lines between stars. He gives it no rite or use. It reached English readers through the J.F. translation (London, 1651) and Francis Barrett's The Magus (London, 1801).

firstAttestation.author: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
firstAttestation.place: [Cologne]. The printer is usually given as Johannes Soter; Eton College's catalogue records the attribution with a query and notes Adams's suggestion of Basel. Catalogues report four or five issues dated 1533.
firstAttestation.locator: Book III, chapter 30. The 1651 English heading is 'Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists'. The Celestial is the top row of a woodcut of three alphabets (Celestial, Malachim, Transitus fluvii). I did not verify the 1533 page or signature.
firstAttestation.notes: This is the earliest printing of this alphabet I could document; I found no earlier exemplar. Agrippa's 1510 manuscript draft, which Trithemius received at St Jakob in Würzburg before 8 April 1510, has not been checked for this chapter. Perrone Compagni's critical edition (Brill, 1992) would settle whether the alphabets were already there. Websites that date the Celestial to 1531 are confusing it with the 1531 printings, which contained Book I only.

transmission.work: De occulta philosophia (manuscript draft dedicated to Trithemius)
transmission.author: Agrippa
transmission.what: The early draft of the work. I have not verified whether it contained the chapter of Hebrew alphabets.

transmission.work: Miqneh Avram / Peculium Abrae (Venice: Daniel Bomberg)
transmission.author: Abraham de Balmes
transmission.what: Context, not the Celestial itself. This grammar prints a ring-letter alphabet called Ketav ever ha-nahar ('script beyond the river') as an example of derivative alphabets. Macfarlane calls it the first printed alphabet of this kind. It is the ancestor of Agrippa's Passing the River.

transmission.work: De occulta philosophia libri tres, III.30 ([Cologne: J. Soter?])
transmission.author: Agrippa
transmission.what: First printing of the Scriptura coelestis that I could document. It is set as a woodcut row naming the Hebrew letters, above the Malachim and Transitus fluvii rows, with one sentence explaining the name.

transmission.work: De originibus seu de Hebraicae linguae et gentis antiquitate (Paris)
transmission.author: Guillaume Postel
transmission.what: Parallel idea, not this alphabet. A bookseller's description of Gaffarel credits Postel with first arguing that the Hebrew letters can be read in the constellations.

transmission.author: Agrippa
transmission.what: A later Latin printing with the passage and the alphabet tables. Travis Shores reproduces the three alphabets from this '1550 reprint', and Source Library hosts a 1550 copy of the passage. Its woodcuts are re-cut, so forms may differ from 1533; I did not compare them.

transmission.work: Thrésor de l'histoire des langues de cest univers (Cologny: Matthieu Berjon; posthumous)
transmission.author: Claude Duret (d. 1611)
transmission.what: Reprints a 'Scriptura Celestis'. Peterson cites it at p. 119 (giving the place as 'Cologne'). A hobby blog places Duret's related Solomonic alphabets at pp. 131-132. The page was not checked against a scan.

transmission.work: Curiositez inouyes sur la sculpture talismanique des Persans, horoscope des Patriarches, et lecture des estoilles (Paris)
transmission.author: Jacques Gaffarel
transmission.what: A different 'celestial writing'. It has two folding planispheres on which the constellations themselves form Hebrew letters, which Gaffarel credits to a 'R. Chomer'. It gave Agrippa's one-line etymology a full theory. English translation by Edmund Chilmead, Unheard-of Curiosities (London: Humphrey Moseley, 1650).

transmission.work: Three Books of Occult Philosophy (London: R.W. for Gregory Moule)
transmission.author: Agrippa, translated by 'J.F.'
transmission.what: English translation of III.30 with the tables re-cut. One cipher site places the Celestial at p. 439; this is unverified.

transmission.author: Thomas Bang (Bangius)
transmission.what: A study of letters and their origins. Macfarlane treats it as a learned response to two things: the Enoch fragments and the idea of celestial writing (above all Gaffarel's) as threats to Christian teaching on angels. The snippets I read characterise Bang's stance in conflicting ways.

transmission.work: The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer (London: Lackington, Allen & Co.)
transmission.author: Francis Barrett
transmission.what: Book II, Part I, chapter XVI ('Another way of making characters, according to the Cabalists') copies Agrippa's text. A plate shows four registers: Theban, Celestial Writing, Malachim, Passing the River. This plate is the version most modern charts copy.

transmission.author: Joseph H. Peterson
transmission.what: Publishes a 'Celestial writing' font taken from De occulta philosophia III (1533), under a CC-BY 4.0 licence as stated on the fonts page.

transmission.work: 'Written in the Stars? Alphabets and Angels in Early Modern Europe', Journal of the History of Ideas 86.3, pp. 473-506
transmission.author: Kirsten Macfarlane
transmission.what: The scholarly account of how Christian scholars came to treat Brillenbuchstaben from medieval Jewish kabbalistic manuscripts as star-derived, angel-authored alphabets.

claims.claim: The Hebrews call this writing 'celestial' because they show it placed and figured among the stars, just as astrologers draw the images of the signs from the lines of the stars.
claims.evidence: This is documented only as Agrippa's report. The Latin (III.30) reads 'quam vocant coelestem, quia inter sydera collocatam ...'. The 1651 English reads 'a writing which they call Celestiall, because they shew it placed and figured amongst the Stars'. That the letters really come from star-figures is a claim Agrippa reports; he does not demonstrate it.
sources: J.F. trans. 1651, III.xxx (Peterson transcription; EEBO A26565)

claims.claim: The letters are formed from the figures of the stars.
claims.evidence: Agrippa's sentence is the only basis for this. It was later built into a theory by Postel (1538) and Gaffarel (1629). No source I found shows that any Celestial letter matches a real constellation.
sources: Peter Harrington catalogue on Gaffarel 1629 (citing Postel 1538)

claims.evidence: Wikipedia and Omniglot say 'created by Agrippa'. Agrippa himself presents it as a script in use 'among the Hebrews' (apud illos). Macfarlane places such ring-ended letters in medieval Jewish kabbalistic manuscripts. No exemplar of this specific alphabet earlier than 1533 has been found, so its maker is unknown.

claims.claim: The Celestial alphabet was made to communicate with angels.
claims.evidence: This is a modern website claim (Wikipedia, Omniglot). In III.30 Agrippa names only the Malachim as 'of Angels, or Regal' and assigns no use to the Celestial. The angelic reading of these scripts belongs to later learned readers (Macfarlane) and to the name 'Malachim'.

claims.claim: Its ring-ended strokes belong to the charaktêres tradition.
claims.evidence: Bohak (2011) shows that ring-letter charaktêres are Graeco-Egyptian in origin and central to Jewish magical texts from Late Antiquity onward. The Rylands posts describe them as signs of angelic scripts (Hebrew ḥotamot, 'seals'). Linking Agrippa's Celestial specifically to this family is a graphic inference supported by Macfarlane's framing, not a stated derivation.
The 1531 printings (Paris, Antwerp, Cologne) contained Book I only. Book III, and with it chapter 30, first appeared in the complete edition of 1533.
sources: Wellcome and Eton catalogue records of the 1533 edition

claims.claim: It is the same as Dee and Kelley's 'Enochian' or 'celestial' alphabet.
claims.evidence: It is not. Enochian (1580s) is a separate alphabet that is sometimes also called 'celestial' or 'angelic'. Wikipedia warns against the confusion.

claims.claim: Grimoires wrote angel names in this alphabet on pentacles.
claims.evidence: This is documented for the sister scripts in Mathers's Key of Solomon (1889): Malachim around a pentacle of Mars and in a conjuration, and Passing the River in the Plate III pentacle. My searches found no grimoire passage that uses the Celestial specifically.
sources: Mathers, Key of Solomon (Esoteric Archives; sacred-texts Plate III)

letters.name: Aleph
letters.form: UNVERIFIED RECONSTRUCTION HINT, NOT AGRIPPA'S FORM AS SEEN: I could not view the 1533 woodcut or any facsimile. This describes the skeleton of the Hebrew square letter that the Celestial letter is reported to resemble, drawn in thin strokes with a small ring (ringlet) at each free stroke-end; most reproductions show open rings, some modern charts fill them as dots. Skeleton: one long diagonal from upper left to lower right; a short upper-right arm dropping from the top right onto the middle of the diagonal; a short lower-left leg rising from the bottom left to the diagonal. Rings at the free tips.
letters.note: The value and order follow the Hebrew alphabet, which the table follows (all sources agree on 22 letters named after the Hebrew letters). The numeric value is the standard Hebrew one; the Celestial table itself is not known to print numbers. Do not draw from this text alone: check the glyph against the 1533 woodcut (Library of Congress copy, archive.org/details/DeOccultaPhilosophiaLoc1533) or Joseph H. Peterson's CC-BY 4.0 'Celestial writing' font, which he says is taken from the 1533 edition.

No image or facsimile was viewable in this environment, and I found no text that describes the glyphs letter by letter. Each 'form' is a low-confidence hint giving the Hebrew square-letter skeleton plus ring-ends. The basis for it is that sources describe the set as Hebrew-derived glyphs with small circles at the extremities, and one encoding draft notes that most Celestial letters clearly resemble their Hebrew counterparts. To draw the letters, use the 1533 woodcut (top row of the three-alphabet figure in III.30; Library of Congress copy on archive.org) or Peterson's CC-BY 4.0 'Celestial writing' font taken from 1533. uses.use: Displayed in Agrippa as one of the Hebrew 'fashions of characters'
uses.evidence: III.30 lists the most ancient Mosaic script (with the remark that the letters in use today were instituted by Esdras), then the Celestial, Malachim and Passing the River, then prints the tables. The chapter then moves on to the Cabalists' 'nine chambers' method of making characters. No rite is attached to the Celestial.

uses.use: Context of characters for spirits and angels in Book III
uses.evidence: It sits between III.29 (characters and seals of spirits, with the Theban letters that Agrippa says Peter of Abano gives as delivered by Honorius of Thebes) and III.31 (marks of spirits received by revelation). This setting is what later readers took as licence to write angel names in it.

uses.use: Learned discussion of the origin of letters
uses.evidence: Duret (1613) reprints it in a history of languages. Gaffarel (1629) develops star-writing into a theory. Bang (1657) responds to the idea of celestial writing (Macfarlane 2025).

uses.evidence: Not documented for the Celestial in the sources I found. Mathers's Key of Solomon (1889) uses Malachim and Passing the River for this. If the site mentions the practice, it should say it is attested for the sister scripts.

cautions: LETTER FORMS ARE UNVERIFIED. Every 'form' is a reconstruction hint based on the Hebrew skeleton. Drawing them as 'Agrippa's Celestial' without checking the 1533 woodcut or Peterson's 1533-based font would present guesses as the source.

Book III, chapter 30 is headed (1651) 'Another manner of making Characters, delivered by Cabalists'. The phrase 'delivered by Angels' belongs to no chapter title I could verify. One search summary placed the passage under 'xxviii' on a Peterson sub-page, which I take to be a misreading, but it should be confirmed against the 1533 scan.
Do not date it 1531: Book III first appeared in 1533.
Do not call it 'invented by Agrippa' or say it was 'used to talk with angels'. Agrippa reports it as a Hebrew script and gives it no use.

Keep it apart from three other things: Dee and Kelley's Enochian (also called 'celestial' or 'angelic'), Gaffarel's 1629 constellation-letters (a different 'celestial writing'), and Postel's 1538 reading of Hebrew letters in the stars.
Later reprints re-cut the table (1550, 1651, Barrett 1801, Duret 1613), so forms may drift between editions. The page should name the edition it follows.
Peterson gives Duret's imprint as 'Cologne, 1613'. Library catalogues give Cologny (near Geneva), 1613, a posthumous edition (Duret died in 1611).
The printer of the 1533 edition is usually given as Johannes Soter of Cologne, but some catalogues query it (Adams suggests Basel).
Reading direction is unsettled (Wikipedia: left to right; dCode: right to left like Hebrew). Left-to-right order in the table is not evidence of writing direction.
Ring-ends: most reproductions show open ringlets and some modern charts show solid dots. Follow the source chosen.
Peterson's transcriptions carry a copyright notice. His fonts page states CC-BY 4.0; confirm the licence for the Celestial font on the page before embedding it, and credit it.
Pages and folios: the 1533 page and signature, the 1651 page (one cipher site says p. 439) and Barrett's plate placement are unverified.

confidence: SOLID: the alphabet is printed in Agrippa's De occulta philosophia III.30 in the complete edition of 1533, with Malachim and Transitus fluvii. Agrippa's one-sentence explanation of the name (the Hebrews show it placed and figured among the stars, as astrologers draw sign-images from star-lines) is solid. So are its 22 letters in Hebrew order, its reprinting in the 1651 English translation and in Barrett's Magus (1801, Book II Part I ch. XVI and plate), and Macfarlane's 2025 placing of such ring-letters in medieval Jewish kabbalistic manuscripts and early modern Christian scholarship. SHAKY: every letter form (none seen; all 22 are low-confidence hints) and all page and folio numbers. Also uncertain: whether the 1510 draft contained the chapter, the exact Latin wording beyond the opening clause, Duret's page (p. 119 per Peterson), Bang's precise stance, any documented use of the Celestial specifically on talismans (found only for its sister scripts), and the reading direction.
